key_insight: LLM confidence reflects two opposing biases: a choice-supportive bias that inflates confidence in an initial answer and a systematic overweighting of contradictory advice that pulls confidence away from optimal Bayesian updating, together explaining instances of both overconfidence and underconfidence.
problem_solved: Explains why large language models are miscalibrated — sometimes overconfident, sometimes underconfident — by identifying and quantifying the competing cognitive-style biases that drive confidence updates after receiving advice.
method: Behavioral-style protocol: elicit an initial answer and confidence from an LLM, present external advice (supporting or contradicting), then measure the updated confidence.
Computational modeling: compare empirical updates to an ideal Bayesian updater and fit models that include a choice-supportive bias and asymmetric weighting of contradictory advice.
Cross-model and condition analysis: test robustness across LLMs, prompt conditions, and advice types to quantify contribution of each bias to miscalibration.
impact: Provides a mechanistic account of confidence errors in LLMs, enabling better calibration, safer human-AI collaboration, and targeted debiasing or uncertainty-estimation strategies for practitioners.
visual_elements: Flow diagram of the experimental trial: Initial answer + initial confidence → external advice (supporting/contradicting) → updated confidence.
Side-by-side bar/violin plots showing overconfidence (choice-supportive) vs underconfidence (overweighting contradictory advice) across conditions.
Schematic comparing empirical update curve to ideal Bayesian updater, highlighting deviations from optimal weighting.
Calibration plot (predicted confidence vs actual accuracy) annotated with contributions from each bias.
paper_title: Competing Biases underlie Overconfidence and Underconfidence in LLMs
paper_authors: Dharshan Kumaran, Stephen M. Fleming, Larisa Markeeva, Joe Heyward, Andrea Banino
